questions.q: A fraud team must find rings of accounts linked through shared devices and addresses across many hops. Data is billions of relationships and queries must return in milliseconds. Which store fits?

options.why: Right: it stores relationships as first-class data and traverses edges directly, so cost follows the neighborhood touched.
Wrong: multi-hop self-joins get slower with depth and Redshift is for reporting, not millisecond lookups.
Wrong: it is built for key lookups, not multi-hop traversals.
Wrong: it stores JSON documents, not relationship paths.

questions.explain: Questions about connections across several hops point to a graph database.
questions.remember: Relationships, highly connected data, fraud rings, social network, knowledge graph → Neptune.
variants: Simple key lookups at scale → DynamoDB.
Reporting with joins → Redshift or Aurora.
JSON documents → DocumentDB.

questions.q: A team has existing Neo4j Cypher queries over a property graph and wants to move to AWS with minimal query rewrites. Which option fits?

options.why: Wrong: SPARQL queries RDF data, not a property graph.
Right: openCypher is a declarative pattern-matching language on the property graph, compatible with Cypher.
Wrong: it works on property graphs but is an imperative traversal language, so every query would be rewritten.
Wrong: it does not scale on deep traversals and needs full rewrites.

questions.explain: Cypher skills map to openCypher on the property graph model.
questions.remember: Neo4j/Cypher → openCypher; TinkerPop step-by-step → Gremlin; RDF, ontology, linked data → SPARQL.
variants: Team uses TinkerPop traversals → Gremlin.
Data is linked open data or ontologies → RDF and SPARQL.
The same property graph can be read with both Gremlin and openCypher.

questions.q: A replica-heavy Neptune cluster has clients on long-lived WebSocket connections. Several hours in, one reader handles nearly all the read traffic although the reader endpoint is used. What is the cause and fix?

options.t: The reader endpoint balances queries, so a replica is broken; reboot it
options.why: Wrong: Neptune does not balance queries at all.

options.t: The reader endpoint balances connections through DNS, so open connections stay on one replica; reconnect and disable DNS caching
options.why: Right: each connection keeps its replica until closed, and cached DNS answers defeat round robin.
Wrong: custom endpoints group instances but do not rebalance existing connections.
Wrong: authentication has no effect on how connections are spread.

questions.explain: The reader endpoint round-robins connections, not queries.
questions.remember: Reader endpoint = connection-level DNS round robin. Long connections and DNS caching cause skew; reconnect and disable DNS caching.
variants: Need query-level balance → spread across instance endpoints in the app.
Isolate analytics from OLTP reads → custom endpoint (up to 5).
Writes must follow failover → cluster endpoint.

questions.q: A production Neptune cluster has a single writer and no replicas. Leadership wants failover to finish in about a minute, even if an AZ fails. What should you do?

options.t: Add one or more replicas in other AZs
options.why: Right: with replicas a replica is promoted, typically under 120 seconds and often under 60; without them the primary is recreated in up to about 10 minutes.
Wrong: storage already keeps six copies across 3 AZs; compute is the gap.
Wrong: snapshots help recovery, not failover time.
Wrong: it targets Region DR and is more than this need.

questions.explain: Storage spans 3 AZs already; compute availability comes from replicas.
questions.remember: No replica → primary recreated (up to ~10 min). With replicas → failover under 120 s. Multi-AZ is not a backup.
variants: Need a specific replica to take over first → promotion tier 0.
Region failure with seconds of lag → Global Database.
After failover apps need retry logic, a new connection and no DNS caching.

questions.q: A company needs low-latency local reads in three Regions and disaster recovery for a Region outage, with storage-level replication lag typically under a second. Which Neptune feature fits?

options.why: Wrong: it gives a higher RPO and is slower to recover.
Wrong: it adds readers inside one Region only.
Right: one primary Region plus up to 5 read-only secondary Regions, replicated at the storage layer typically under 1 second.
Wrong: it is an in-memory analytics engine, not a DR feature.

questions.explain: Global Database is the low-lag multi-Region option.
questions.remember: Seconds of lag, local reads, Region DR → Global Database (5 secondary Regions). Cheap, cold DR → snapshot copy.
variants: Cheap cold DR with higher RPO → copy snapshots to another Region.
Secondary clusters cannot use auto scaling and t3/t4g.medium is not supported.
Region outage → detach and promote a secondary.

questions.q: An auditor requires encryption at rest on an existing, unencrypted Neptune cluster. What is the correct approach?

options.t: Enable KMS encryption on the running cluster
options.why: Wrong: encryption can only be chosen at creation, not in place.

options.t: Modify the instances to use TLS
options.why: Wrong: TLS is encryption in transit and is already required.

options.t: Take a snapshot, copy it with encryption, and restore a new cluster
options.why: Right: this is the only path from unencrypted to encrypted; the restore creates a new cluster.
Wrong: it controls who can connect, not storage encryption.

questions.explain: Encrypt by snapshot, encrypted copy, then restore.
questions.remember: Neptune encryption at rest (KMS) is set at creation; to change, snapshot → copy with encryption → restore.
variants: Recover from accidental deletes → PITR to a new cluster within retention.
Long retention beyond 35 days → manual snapshots.
Need no passwords in the app → IAM authentication with SigV4.

questions.q: A load of billions of rows from S3 into Neptune fails. The role has S3 read access and files are valid CSV. Which two causes are the most likely? (Choose two.)

options.t: The VPC has no S3 gateway VPC endpoint
options.why: Right: the loader runs inside the VPC and needs an S3 VPC endpoint.

options.t: The files are encrypted with SSE-C
options.why: Right: the loader supports SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS but not SSE-C.
Wrong: single-file gzip and bzip2 are supported.
Wrong: UTF-8 is the required encoding.

questions.explain: Loader needs the IAM role, S3 VPC endpoint, supported format and non-SSE-C encryption.
questions.remember: Loader failures: missing role, missing S3 VPC endpoint, wrong Region, bad format, SSE-C, or .zip/.tar archives.
variants: Files are .zip → not supported; use .gz or .bz2 single files.
Slow load → temporary larger writer, split files, same-Region bucket.
Loader is not ACID.

questions.q: A Neptune bill is dominated by per-million I/O request charges on a busy cluster. Which change cuts the cost while keeping the cluster?

options.why: Wrong: it changes compute billing, not the per-I/O charge.
Right: it removes the per-I/O charge for a higher instance and storage price; it needs engine 1.3.0.0+ and can be switched once per 30 days.
Wrong: more instances raise cost and do not remove per-I/O charges.
Wrong: Streams add I/O and storage cost.

questions.remember: I/O a large part of the bill → I/O-Optimized (once per 30 days). Standard pays per million I/O.
variants: Spiky or dev/test compute → Serverless or t4g.medium.
Storage is billed on the high-water mark.
Idle dev/test cluster → stop it.

questions.q: A Neptune workload has unpredictable spikes lasting a few minutes each day and the team does not want to plan capacity. Which design fits?

options.t: Provisioned r6g instances sized for the peak
options.why: Wrong: they are billed hourly all day and require capacity planning.
Wrong: burstable classes are for dev/test only.

options.t: Neptune Serverless with a generous maximum NCU
options.why: Right: compute scales in NCUs (1 NCU = 2 GiB) between your min and max, billed per second.
Wrong: it is an in-memory analytics engine, not an OLTP database.

questions.remember: Spiky or unknown load → Serverless. Too low min or max NCU causes timeouts; tier 0-1 readers scale with the writer.
variants: Slow steady read growth → read-replica auto scaling on CPU.
Graph algorithms on tens of billions of edges → Neptune Analytics.
BufferCacheHitRatio below 99.9% → bigger memory instance.

questions.q: Latency on a provisioned Neptune cluster rises, and `BufferCacheHitRatio` is 97%. What is the best fix?

options.t: Move to a larger, more memory-rich instance class
options.why: Right: the graph working set does not fit in the buffer cache; below 99.9% means scale up.
Wrong: replicas do not enlarge the writer's cache and the same-class rule still applies.
Wrong: Streams add I/O and slightly reduce write performance.
Wrong: it hides timeouts but does not fix cache misses.

questions.explain: A low cache hit ratio means too little memory.
questions.remember: BufferCacheHitRatio below 99.9% → bigger instance. Resize the writer by creating a bigger replica and failing over.
variants: Many pending requests or 429 throttling → add capacity or smooth load.
Serverless timeouts → raise min and max NCU.
UndoLogListSize keeps growing → upgrade the writer.
